content:
The Sub-Committee considered a request to
install CCTV in a licensed vehicle.
 
It was noted that Tandridge District Council
did not mandate the installation of CCTV in all licensed
vehicles.  It was therefore a matter for
individuals to request the Licensing Authority’s approval to
install CCTV in their licensed vehicle(s).
 
The applicant had decided not to attend the
hearing and instead chose to rely on the content of their written
request and their further written submission, as included in a
supplementary agenda pack for the meeting.
 
The Licensing Officer presented the report to
the Sub-Committee and explained the background to the
request.  The Licensing Officer stated
that it was for the Sub-Committee to decide whether to agree to the
request, to determine any limitations should it be minded to agree
to the request, and to impose any appropriate conditions.
 
The Sub-Committee noted the applicant’s
reasons for the request, in particular his concern for his and his
passengers’ safety, following a number of incidents.
 
In response to questions from the
Sub-Committee, the following information was provided:
 
·      
Recording equipment had to comply with the standards set out by the
Information Commissioner’s Office.  There were a number of suppliers in the
marketplace that provided specialist equipment to owners of
licensed vehicles.

 
·      
Recording equipment was not accessible by the applicant. It could
only be accessed by the local operator named on the written
request.  The operator would be the
designated data controller in accordance with the requirements of
the GDPR.  The local operator was
already registered as a data controller with the Information
Commissioner’s Office as they handled individuals’
personal data to facilitate the minicab bookings that they
made.
 
·      
The local operator had not been the subject of any complaints since
they were established in 2023.  The
operator’s owner had accrued approximately ten years’
experience.
 
·      
Footage would be the subject of a minimum retention period and
could be requested at any time by the Licensing Authority and other
authorised bodies or individuals such as the police.  The capturing of sound was ‘by
exception’ and only when activated by either the customer or
the applicant.
 
·      
Conditions would govern the use of recording equipment, in
particular requiring its use at all times that the vehicle was
being used for professional purposes. 
This would not include occasions when it was being used as a
private conveyance by the applicant. 
 
·      
Licensing Officers considered the applicant to be a ‘fit and
proper’ person, with him having received no convictions
including for driving related matters.
 
·      
Determining the limitations of any agreement was a matter for the
Licensing Sub-Committee i.e. it could limit its agreement to
install CCTV to a specified vehicle, a specified vehicle and any
vehicle that replaced it, or for any vehicle used by the
applicant.
 
·      
Failure to comply with the conditions of the agreement could result
in the applicant’s licence being reviewed by the Licensing
Authority.
 
The hearing closed at 10.27am and Licensing
Officers left the meeting room while the Sub-Committee deliberated
on its decision.
 
At the conclusion of the Sub-Committee’s
deliberations, Licensing Officers were called back into the Council
Chamber to be informed of its decision.
 
Councillor Allen requested that his decision
to abstain from voting, citing that he did not have enough
information to enable him to form a view, be noted.
 
Notes on the Sub-Committee’s
deliberations:
 
·      
The Sub-Committee, whilst noting that applicants could not be
compelled to attend hearings, asked Licensing Officers to encourage
their attendance in order to help inform the Sub-Committee’s
consideration of their requests.
 
·      
The Sub-Committee requested that Licensing Officers give
consideration to whether a policy for similar future requests was
worth developing.
 
The decision of the
Sub-Committee was:
 
1.    
To grant the request install CCTV for up to one of the
applicant’s vehicles at any one time, subject to the
conditions set out in the schedule attached to these minutes.

 
2.    
That in the event the applicant replaced his vehicle and wished to
install CCTV within it, the conditions set out in the schedule be
applied to the applicant’s replacement vehicle.
 
Note on the Sub-Committee’s decision:
The Sub-Committee wished to clarify that any additional licensed
vehicle used by the applicant in pursuance of his business, should
he wish to install CCTV within it, would require another request to
be made to the Licensing Authority.
topline: The Sub-Committee has decided to grant the request to install CCTV in a licensed vehicle, subject to specific conditions.

On Thursday 7 May 2026 elections will be held
for East Surrey Council. On the same day a County Council
By-Election will take place in Warlingham and a Neighbourhood
Planning Referendum (NPR) will take place for Caterham, Chaldon and
Whyteleafe.
The current Polling Station for Whyteleafe East (WAW2) is
Warlingham Community Library. This Polling Place is also the
Polling Place for Warlingham West (WAW1).
Voters in WAW1 will be voting in the Warlingham Ward of East Surrey
Council and in a Council By-Election for the Warlingham Division.
Voters in WAW2 will be voting in the Caterham Valley Ward of East
Surrey Council and the NPR.
Moving the polling station for WAW2 to St Luke's Church Whyteleafe
will reduce the number of different ballot papers and ballot boxes
at Warlingham Community Library. St Luke's is the polling station
for WHT1, which will be voting in the same polls. Voters in WAW2
voter at St Luke's Church for the by-election held in October
2025.

·

An overview of the CAT programme was provided,

criteria for Committee approval in principle. Assets approved in
principle would move to detailed due diligence and subsequently to
contract, subject to no material issues arising. Members noted that
assets classified as “complex” varied in the nature of
the issues involved, which could include trust arrangements,
unregistered land, or timelines driven by external bodies such as
the Charity Commission.
 
During the debate, Officers confirmed that
land held in trust or unregistered land was classified as more
complex due to the regulatory or procedural steps involved, rather
than any underlying ownership concerns.
 
Members expressed concerns regarding the
recommendation for South Godstone Playing Field and Pavilion (Item
2e), namely that, as expressions of interest had been received from
both Godstone Parish Council and the South Godstone Sports and
Community Association, that the recommendation was to allow
approval in principle to either party.

·        
both Godstone Parish Council and the South Godstone Sports and
Community Association had undergone the standard due diligence
scoring process and were both considered suitable recipients for
the asset;

required.

proceed to a vote on recommendation 2e at this meeting, with an
update on recipient preference to be provided verbally at the
Strategy & Resources Committee meeting due to take place on 29
January 2026

The Committee received a report which set out
the proposed six-week Regulation 18 Issues & Options
consultation as the first stage towards developing a new Local
Plan.
 
There was recognition that the resulting Local
Plan will need to balance housing, infrastructure and economic
development needs with protection of the district’s character
and landscape.
 
The consultation document included:

·        
an introduction to the need for a Local Plan and the national
policy context;

·        
a portrait of the district and its key constraints;

·        
a draft vision for the district to 2044;

·        
high?level options for the locational
strategy;

·        
sections including affordable housing, infrastructure, the historic
and natural environment, health and wellbeing, and sustainable
design;
 
The consultation would be supported by a
summary document to encourage wider engagement and an online
questionnaire, which could be saved and completed in stages.
 
In response to Members questions, it was
confirmed that:
 

·        
the aim was to provide balanced, accessible information without any
decisions to be taken on specific sites or strategies at this early
stage;

·        
terminology such as “locally valued landscapes” could
be clarified to ensure residents understood that Areas of Great
Landscape Value (AGLV) were included;

·        
the draft did not refer to the draft National Planning Policy
Framework that is out for separate consultation.  It was agreed to add reference to this in the
Issues and Options document.

·        
the draft vision was aspirational, and additional text could be
considered in future iterations to explain deliverability and the
Council’s reliance on external infrastructure partners;

·        
explanatory wording or short definitions (e.g. Section 106) could
be added where helpful;

·        
infrastructure delivery planning would involve formal engagement
with transport, health and other statutory providers; and

·        
consideration would be given to whether photographs in the document
could be labelled.
 
 
 
R E S O L V E
D– that the Local Plan Issues and Options
Consultation document in Appendix A of the Agenda pack is released,
for the prescribed 6-week period, under Regulation 18 of the Town
and Country Planning (Local Planning) Regulations 2012.
topline: The Planning Policy Committee has decided to approve recommendations for a six-week Regulation 18 Issues & Options consultation to develop a new Local Plan.

content:
As a public speaker was in attendance in
relation to Agenda Item 6 (Proposed Article 4 for smaller HMOs),
the Committee agreed to discuss Agenda Item 6, ahead of Agenda Item
5 (Local Plan Issues and Options).   
 
Officers presented a proposal to introduce an
immediate Article 4 Direction, covering Whyteleafe, Caterham Valley
and Caterham Hill  thereby removing
permitted development rights that currently allow for the change of
use from Use Class C3 (Dwellinghouses) to Use Class C4 (small
Houses in Multiple Occupation) without planning permission.
 
The proposed action followed consideration of
evidence showing a marked increase in small HMOs, within the
defined areas, in the last year compared to previous
years.  The resulting impacts included
reduced housing quality, pressure on residential amenities, loss of
family housing, parking congestion, increased noise and anti-social
behaviour.  There had been a steady
increase of complaints to Planning Enforcement and Licencing and
growing concerns from Councillors and residents.
 
Evidence demonstrated that the scale and speed
of change meant that a non-immediate direction would not offer
sufficient protection as it would allow uncontrolled conversions
for a further 12 months.  An immediate
direction was therefore deemed necessary and proportionate.
 
Trudy Miles, a Whyteleafe resident, addressed
the committee in relation to concerns about small HMOs and
potential unauthorised developments in Whyteleafe.
 
In response to Member questions, it was
confirmed that the current legal advice was that:

·        
the Direction becomes effective from the date of issue, including
during the 21?day consultation period;

·        
the final decision must return to Committee within the
six?month statutory window in order for the
Direction to remain in force;

·        
a timeline for issuing the Direction would be provided once legal
advice on preparation timeframes had been confirmed;

·        
the scope could not be extended at this stage due to insufficient
evidence to meet national policy tests, but data would continue to
be monitored and further phases explored;

·        
work was underway with Licensing colleagues to review HMO licensing
thresholds and enforcement of unlicensed HMOs;
 
Members would be kept updated on progress and
milestone timings.
 
R E S O L V E
D  – that:
 
1.   
Authority be given to the Deputy Chief Executive, in consultation
with the Chair of the Committee, to start the legal process to make
an immediate Article 4 Direction removing Use Class C4 permitted
development rights for small HMO’s (up to 6 people) in
Caterham Valley, Caterham Hill and Whyteleafe areas, and to
undertake the statutory publicity and consultation required under
the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development)
(England) Order 2015.

 
2.   
The Deputy Chief Executive be required to bring a further report
back to the Planning Policy Committee, following the statutory
consultation period, enabling the Committee to consider any
representations received and determine whether to confirm the
Direction.
topline: The Planning Policy Committee has decided to introduce an immediate Article 4 Direction to remove permitted development rights for small HMOs in certain areas.

content:
The report included information about the key
planning indicators for quarter 2. The Council was required to
submit the data quarterly to the Ministry of Housing, Communities
and Local Government. It also contained information about the
current planning applications. Performance reports were presented
to each policy committee at the end of each quarter. The following
points were highlighted by the Interim Head of Planning:

The percentage of decisions on major
applications made within 13 weeks or within the agreed extension of
time for Q2 was 100%.
The percentage of decisions on minor
applications made within 8 weeks or within the agreed extension of
time for Q2 was 96%.
The percentage of decisions on other
applications made within 8 weeks or within the agreed extension of
time for Q2 was 93%.
During Q2, there were 175 decisions,
11 minor applications were refused as the decision was not
determined in the timeframe.
The validation timescales had
substantially reduced since the summer and currently applications
were being checked for validation within one week of receipt.

 
R E S O L V E
D – that the Committee noted the Quarter 2 2025/26
Performance Indicators for the Planning Policy Committee.
topline: The Planning Policy Committee has decided to review the Quarter 2 2025/26 Performance Indicators.
